title: A good prediction still needs a useful action
lead: NTT evaluates action outcomes before stacking objects. In Bologna experiments, information that improved cable-shape prediction did not always improve control.

news.title: NTT screens robot actions before stacking cargo
news.summary: NTT presented a model that predicts falls and collisions before a robot executes a movement. In a small shelf-stacking experiment, the company reported success rising from 73.1% to 92.3%.
news.details: On November 11, NTT presented a world model: software that predicts how a robot's surroundings will change after an action. It takes several candidate actions from a controller, generates an outcome for each and evaluates the risk of objects falling or a stack collapsing. NTT's physical-control adapter is incorporated into a video-generation model. It estimates object position, orientation, speed and mass from images, then uses equations of motion. This calculation is intended to constrain prediction errors such as objects disappearing during collisions. The description comes from the developer; it is not independent validation of the inferred mass or other properties.

Reproduction therefore depends on both the cost of scoring candidate actions and the method used to infer physical properties from images. Improved stacking success alone does not establish whether screening can keep pace with a particular baggage line.
news.limitations: NTT reports a small shelf-stacking experiment. Operation with varied baggage at an active airport is not established, and numerical action-screening latency is not provided.
news.evidence_status: Official company announcement; the reported results and estimates are not independent verification.
news.body:
A gripper reaching its destination does not guarantee a successful placement: the neighboring stack might become unstable. NTT adds consequence prediction to existing robot control. A controller first proposes actions, and a separate model compares their predicted outcomes. Generating a movement and evaluating what it will cause remain distinct functions within the system.

On November 11, NTT presented a world model: software that predicts how a robot's surroundings will change after an action. It takes several candidate actions from a controller, generates an outcome for each and evaluates the risk of objects falling or a stack collapsing. NTT's physical-control adapter is incorporated into a video-generation model. It estimates object position, orientation, speed and mass from images, then uses equations of motion. This calculation is intended to constrain prediction errors such as objects disappearing during collisions. The description comes from the developer; it is not independent validation of the inferred mass or other properties.

NTT tested the approach with a small robot performing a shelf-stacking task intended to imitate cargo stacking. Reported success increased from 73.1% without the technology to 92.3% with it. Those figures describe the company's test rig, not baggage handling at an operating airport. A separate evaluation compared predicted and reference videos in scenes containing collisions between multiple objects. Airport baggage is the first intended application, with field demonstrations involving Mujin still ahead. NTT also plans to exhibit the research on November 18–25. The announcement therefore contains an experimental result and a deployment plan at different stages of maturity.

The release describes operation fast enough for integration into robot control, but supplies no numerical prediction latency. Reproduction therefore depends on both the cost of scoring candidate actions and the method used to infer physical properties from images. Improved stacking success alone does not establish whether screening can keep pace with a particular baggage line.

news.title: Atlas wheels expose the demands on actuator models
news.summary: Boston Dynamics turned Atlas into a wheeled research testbed. The team examined whether movements learned in simulation matched the capabilities of real actuators.
news.details: Boston Dynamics described its wheeled Atlas experiment on November 9. Controls engineer Andy Wu stresses that the humanoid with its feet replaced by wheels is a research testbed, not a new commercial configuration. An off-the-shelf scooter rim is attached to the existing ankle actuator through a custom adapter. In the computer model, the corresponding joint can rotate continuously. Accelerating, turning and braking require the motors to deliver speed and torque together under load. Torque is the turning effort produced by a drive. The team wanted those demanding operating conditions to test both the actuators and their mathematical models.

Controls engineer Andy Wu stresses that the humanoid with its feet replaced by wheels is a research testbed, not a new commercial configuration. An off-the-shelf scooter rim is attached to the existing ankle actuator through a custom adapter. In the computer model, the corresponding joint can rotate continuously. Accelerating, turning and braking require the motors to deliver speed and torque together under load. Torque is the turning effort produced by a drive. The team wanted those demanding operating conditions to test both the actuators and their mathematical models.
news.engineering_impact: The team adjusted rewards, command ranges and posture handling using an existing training framework. The account does not quantify the contribution of each adjustment. Wu names actuator-failure response as work he has started; he does not present it as an already demonstrated ability of this wheeled robot to continue safely after a drive fails.
news.limitations: Boston Dynamics describes wheeled Atlas as a research testbed. It provides no service-life measurement under these loads and does not present drive-failure response as an already validated capability.
news.evidence_status: Official company announcement; the reported results and estimates are not independent verification.
news.body:
The most visible modification, wheels in place of feet, serves a specific experimental purpose. Continuous loaded rotation exposes motor behavior that an idealized simulator might omit. The account is valuable as an example of matching actuator models to learned whole-body control, rather than as an announcement of a new locomotion product for customers.

Boston Dynamics described its wheeled Atlas experiment on November 9. Controls engineer Andy Wu stresses that the humanoid with its feet replaced by wheels is a research testbed, not a new commercial configuration. An off-the-shelf scooter rim is attached to the existing ankle actuator through a custom adapter. In the computer model, the corresponding joint can rotate continuously. Accelerating, turning and braking require the motors to deliver speed and torque together under load. Torque is the turning effort produced by a drive. The team wanted those demanding operating conditions to test both the actuators and their mathematical models.

Whole-body control was trained using reinforcement learning: software tries movements in simulation and receives numerical rewards for the resulting behavior. To make the learned movements feasible on hardware, the team characterized the real actuators, tuned the simulated motor model and checked that low-level control settings agreed across software setups. Some behaviors followed human motion recordings. A full-turn jump tracked one such recording, while a sideways dash used wheel rolling where a person would slide their feet. The account demonstrates behavior transferred to hardware, but supplies no comparative endurance protocol or quantified failure-rate evaluation.

The team adjusted rewards, command ranges and posture handling using an existing training framework. The account does not quantify the contribution of each adjustment. Wu names actuator-failure response as work he has started; he does not present it as an already demonstrated ability of this wheeled robot to continue safely after a drive fails.

news.title: Robot lighting test reveals a camera-setting confound
news.summary: A fysical.ai researcher compared four arm controllers after an 11.5-fold illuminance drop. The cameras largely preserved image brightness, so the experiment does not test controller performance on genuinely dark frames.
news.details: Simon Cowling of Denmark-based fysical.ai posted a preliminary research paper on November 10 about testing robot control under different lighting conditions. Four controllers were trained on the same 50 demonstrations: an SO-101 arm had to place a green ball in a basket while ignoring two red balls. Each controller was tested at ten ball placements in normal and dimmed conditions. Workspace illuminance fell from about 520 to 45 lux, an 11.5-fold reduction. The main comparison contained 80 attempts. Success totaled 20 out of 40 attempts in normal light and 19 out of 40 in low light.
news.technical_novelty: Simon Cowling of Denmark-based fysical.ai posted a preliminary research paper on November 10 about testing robot control under different lighting conditions. Four controllers were trained on the same 50 demonstrations: an SO-101 arm had to place a green ball in a basket while ignoring two red balls. Each controller was tested at ten ball placements in normal and dimmed conditions. Workspace illuminance fell from about 520 to 45 lux, an 11.5-fold reduction. The main comparison contained 80 attempts. Success totaled 20 out of 40 attempts in normal light and 19 out of 40 in low light.
news.engineering_impact: Camera settings were read after the experiments, and exposure was not locked during comparison. Isolating its causal contribution would require a separate controlled test with specified settings. Normal and low light were also tested on different days in the same policy order, leaving day and order effects inseparable from lighting in this design.
news.limitations: Simon Cowling tested one rig and one task. Exposure was not locked, settings were read afterward and there was no automatic-exposure-off comparison; day and controller-order effects were not isolated either.
news.evidence_status: Research and author-run experiments; independent reproduction has not been confirmed.
news.body:
For visual robot control, tabletop illuminance and the data entering a policy are different quantities. Cowling shows how widely they can diverge on an ordinary low-cost rig. A light meter recorded substantial dimming, while the cameras did not record a proportionally darker scene. Ignoring the recordings would change the apparent meaning of the controller comparison.

Simon Cowling of Denmark-based fysical.ai posted a preliminary research paper on November 10 about testing robot control under different lighting conditions. Four controllers were trained on the same 50 demonstrations: an SO-101 arm had to place a green ball in a basket while ignoring two red balls. Each controller was tested at ten ball placements in normal and dimmed conditions. Workspace illuminance fell from about 520 to 45 lux, an 11.5-fold reduction. The main comparison contained 80 attempts. Success totaled 20 out of 40 attempts in normal light and 19 out of 40 in low light.

Yet average recorded image brightness fell by only 3% for the front camera and 19% for the wrist camera. After the experiments, the author found automatic exposure enabled: the camera adjusts how it gathers light. This probably compensated for much of the dimming, although its causal role was not tested separately. The results therefore do not establish that the controllers withstand genuinely dark images. The study used one rig and one task, with manually placed balls and a single unblinded scorer. Small trial counts leave substantial uncertainty: the confidence interval for the pooled success change runs from a 23-percentage-point decrease to a 19-point increase.

Camera settings were read after the experiments, and exposure was not locked during comparison. Isolating its causal contribution would require a separate controlled test with specified settings. Normal and low light were also tested on different days in the same policy order, leaving day and order effects inseparable from lighting in this design.

news.title: Cable prediction and action selection favor different information
news.summary: University of Bologna researchers compared ways to represent cable properties during manipulation. Information that improved deformation prediction did not necessarily improve the selected control action.
news.details: University of Bologna researchers posted preliminary work on November 10 on shaping a flexible cable on a plane. Their Geometry–Pointer–Flow method first chooses a segment to grasp, then generates its translation and rotation. The team compared information about cable stiffness and surface friction with a different representation: a learned record of up to five previous actions and the shape changes they produced. Each representation was evaluated separately for predicting the next shape and selecting an action. In simulation, estimated physical parameters improved prediction, but produced no detectable control improvement over a version using geometry alone.
news.technical_novelty: University of Bologna researchers posted preliminary work on November 10 on shaping a flexible cable on a plane. Their Geometry–Pointer–Flow method first chooses a segment to grasp, then generates its translation and rotation. The team compared information about cable stiffness and surface friction with a different representation: a learned record of up to five previous actions and the shape changes they produced. Each representation was evaluated separately for predicting the next shape and selecting an action. In simulation, estimated physical parameters improved prediction, but produced no detectable control improvement over a version using geometry alone.
news.engineering_impact: The task is planar cable shaping with one grasp per action. The experiments do not identify exactly which hidden properties the interaction history encodes. The authors promise code after acceptance, limiting present reproduction to the published description. Success in this setting cannot automatically be transferred to knot tying or three-dimensional cable assembly.
news.limitations: The Bologna study tests planar cable shaping with one grasp per action. Manual reset prevents identical starting shapes; the exact content of the learned history representation is not established, and code is promised after acceptance.
news.evidence_status: Research and author-run experiments; independent reproduction has not been confirmed.
news.body:
Accurately predicting the next cable shape does not guarantee choosing a useful movement. The Bologna study evaluates these objectives separately with a common grasp-selection architecture. This distinction matters experimentally: prediction is scored against the resulting deformation, whereas control is scored by executing the selected action and measuring the shape it actually produces relative to a target.

University of Bologna researchers posted preliminary work on November 10 on shaping a flexible cable on a plane. Their Geometry–Pointer–Flow method first chooses a segment to grasp, then generates its translation and rotation. The team compared information about cable stiffness and surface friction with a different representation: a learned record of up to five previous actions and the shape changes they produced. Each representation was evaluated separately for predicting the next shape and selecting an action. In simulation, estimated physical parameters improved prediction, but produced no detectable control improvement over a version using geometry alone.

The interaction-history version reduced executed one-step shape error by 9.9% across 470 paired simulation trials. Hardware tests covered three cable compliance levels and two support surfaces. Controllers were trained only in simulation, without real-world training or fine-tuning. Within ten actions, the history-based version reached a mean shape error of at most 10 mm in 88.3% of trials, compared with 76.7% for geometry alone. Each controller completed 60 such rollouts. Error means the average distance between corresponding cable and target points, not the largest deviation. Manual resetting prevented exactly identical starting configurations across controllers.

The task is planar cable shaping with one grasp per action. The experiments do not identify exactly which hidden properties the interaction history encodes. The authors promise code after acceptance, limiting present reproduction to the published description. Success in this setting cannot automatically be transferred to knot tying or three-dimensional cable assembly.

news.title: Hachioji construction simulation adds robots that wait for traffic
news.summary: Space Data added workers and robots to a crane simulation set around Hachioji Junction. It describes vehicle-position prediction 2.5 seconds ahead, without claiming physical construction-site trials.
news.details: On November 12, Space Data presented a new scene for RobotBrain, its environment for evaluating robots before deployment. A hypothetical construction yard occupies digitally recreated terrain around Hachioji Junction in Japan. It contains four cranes, six construction vehicles, ten workers and fourteen robots. Ten robots are bipedal and four transport materials. These are simulated participants, not a workforce already operating at the junction. Users can change participant counts and roles to study shared movement in a confined yard. Compared with the company's first crane example, the stated addition is people and robots carrying out different assigned tasks.
news.technical_novelty: On November 12, Space Data presented a new scene for RobotBrain, its environment for evaluating robots before deployment. A hypothetical construction yard occupies digitally recreated terrain around Hachioji Junction in Japan. It contains four cranes, six construction vehicles, ten workers and fourteen robots. Ten robots are bipedal and four transport materials. These are simulated participants, not a workforce already operating at the junction. news.engineering_impact: Agreement with a pendulum calculation cannot be turned into a general accuracy score for robot behavior or shared-work safety. The release provides no validation of these interaction rules against trajectories from an operating construction site. Planning use would require distinguishing public equipment specifications from developer-estimated parameters, especially where those assumptions affect the outcome.
news.limitations: Space Data shows a hypothetical yard, not physical construction trials. Equipment models are unofficial and include estimated parameters; safe simulated movement does not validate a real robot’s safety.
news.evidence_status: Official company announcement; the reported results and estimates are not independent verification.
news.body:
A shared-work simulation needs explicit interaction rules: who yields and where movement is prohibited. Space Data’s construction example supplies such rules inside a hypothetical site. This adds substance beyond showing cranes alone, but recognizable terrain does not establish that digital participants reproduce the behavior of real workers, vehicles and robot controllers under operational conditions.

On November 12, Space Data presented a new scene for RobotBrain, its environment for evaluating robots before deployment. A hypothetical construction yard occupies digitally recreated terrain around Hachioji Junction in Japan. It contains four cranes, six construction vehicles, ten workers and fourteen robots. Ten robots are bipedal and four transport materials. These are simulated participants, not a workforce already operating at the junction. Users can change participant counts and roles to study shared movement in a confined yard. Compared with the company's first crane example, the stated addition is people and robots carrying out different assigned tasks.

According to the developer, a simulated robot anticipates a vehicle's position 2.5 seconds ahead and waits for it to pass. Robots avoid suspended loads, while vehicles stop in front of people. The system calculates load weight, cable tension and load swing. For a 40-meter cable, the reported oscillation period is 12.87 seconds, compared with 12.69 seconds from a pendulum formula. That comparison checks one physical behavior; it does not establish safety for the entire yard. Space Data explicitly says the construction scenario is hypothetical, equipment models are not official manufacturer models and some unpublished parameters are estimates.

Agreement with a pendulum calculation cannot be turned into a general accuracy score for robot behavior or shared-work safety. The release provides no validation of these interaction rules against trajectories from an operating construction site. Planning use would require distinguishing public equipment specifications from developer-estimated parameters, especially where those assumptions affect the outcome.

technology_signal.title: A good prediction still needs a useful action
technology_signal.summary: NTT evaluates action outcomes before stacking objects. In Bologna experiments, information that improved cable-shape prediction did not always improve control.
technology_signal.implications: NTT checked advance screening through actual stacking success on a small rig. The Bologna study separately measures prediction error and the shape produced by an executed action; those outcomes are not interchangeable.
